1.5a:c6d7d9de81a9da822f5ec4ffdf037e88880.text: Following the November 2020 announcement that Tesla would join the S&P 500, the company’s share price experienced a massive surge as institutional investors and index funds rushed to acquire the stock ahead of its official inclusion on December 21. This inclusion propelled Tesla's market capitalization past the $600 billion mark, cementing its status as the most valuable automaker in the world despite producing a fraction of the vehicles manufactured by its legacy competitors. In the months that followed, Tesla capitalized on its soaring stock valuation by announcing stock splits and raising capital, while simultaneously expanding its global manufacturing footprint with the construction of new Gigafactories in Berlin and Texas. However, by early 2021, the stock entered a period of high volatility and correction as rising Treasury yields and broader market rotation pressured high-growth technology and automotive stocks. Despite these market fluctuations, the company continued to report record vehicle deliveries and sustained profitability, validating its integration into the benchmark index and its long-term market dominance.
